definition: Proscribe means to condemn and outlaw at once, branding the practice a public wrong.

Restrict is far milder than proscribe: a restricted practice carries no shame at all — it continues, just inside tighter bounds — while a proscribed one is outlawed entirely and carries public shame.
Prohibit stops just short of proscribe: both put a thing off limits, but proscribe adds public condemnation — the practice is not merely barred but denounced as a wrong.

To outlaw a thing is to strip it of the law's protection — banned, full stop, with penalties waiting. Proscribe reaches further: beyond outlawing, it publicly condemns, branding the practice a wrong. A city can outlaw parking on Main Street without anyone calling parking shameful.

A ban is the blunt, everyday word for an official no — the pool bans glass, the airline bans smoking. Proscribe is heavier artillery: the thing is outlawed and publicly condemned, shame attached. Use proscribe when a code does not just refuse a practice but denounces it.

When the amateur cycling league rewrote its charter, everyone expected tighter rules on hidden motors.
The league went further and chose to proscribe mechanical doping outright.
The new charter does two things at once: it forbids hidden motors under penalty of a lifetime expulsion, and it declares the practice a fraud upon the sport itself.
Riders caught are not quietly fined; they are named in the league's bulletin, and their results are struck.
